The Soviet Collapse

Detente, Afghanistan, Reagan, and Solidarity

Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

For almost thirty years the Cold War had seemed a fixed fact. In the 1970s both sides tried to ease it. By 1980 it had grown harsh again, and a new set of events had begun that would end it. This lesson follows the years of detente, the Soviet war in Afghanistan, the rise of Solidarity in Poland, and Reagan’s policy toward Moscow. As you read, begin a list of the pressures on the Soviet system, and mark which came from outside and which from within. You will need it for this module’s discussion: did Reagan win the Cold War, or did the Soviet Union lose it?

Objectives
  1. Explain what detente achieved and what it did not.
  2. Describe the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the American response.
  3. Explain the rise of Solidarity in Poland and how Reagan’s policies changed the Cold War.

Historical Figure
Leonid BrezhnevLAY-oh-NEED BREZH-nef

Leonid Brezhnev (1906 to 1982) was born in Ukraine and trained as an engineer before rising through the Communist Party. In 1964 he helped to remove Khrushchev and became the head of the party. He ruled for eighteen years, and he put stability first. Few officials lost their jobs, and few reforms were tried.

The Soviet Union grew more powerful abroad under Brezhnev, but it slowed at home. Farms and factories fell behind the West, and the leaders grew old. In his last years Brezhnev was often ill and had to be helped through public ceremonies. When he died in 1982, many of his colleagues were nearly as old as he was.

A Short War?

Historical Figure
John Paul IIJON PAWL the SEK-und

Karol Wojtyla (1920 to 2005) grew up in Poland. In the Second World War he worked in a quarry and studied for the priesthood in secret, because the Germans had closed the seminaries. He became a priest, a professor of philosophy, and the archbishop of Krakow, where he dealt with the Communist government for years.

He was elected pope in 1978 and took the name John Paul II. He traveled more widely than any pope before him, and he spoke often about human dignity and religious freedom. In 1981 a gunman shot him in Saint Peter’s Square, and he survived. He died in 2005, and was declared a saint in 2014.

Historical Figure
Lech WalesaLEK vah-WEN-sah

Lech Walesa (born 1943) was an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk. He had been fired in 1976 for his work with the workers’ cause, and in 1980 he climbed over the shipyard wall to join the strike. He helped to lead it to the Gdansk Agreement. He was a good speaker, blunt and brave, and workers trusted him.

He led Solidarity until the martial law of 1981, when he was interned for eleven months. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983. In 1989 he helped negotiate the end of Communist rule, and in 1990 he was elected president of Poland. He lost the office in 1995.

The Shipyard
Historical Figure
Ronald ReaganRON-ald RAY-gun

Ronald Reagan (1911 to 2004) was born in Illinois and worked as a radio announcer and film actor. He led the actors’ union, and in the 1950s he turned from the Democratic to the Republican Party. He served as governor of California from 1967 to 1975, and he won the presidency in 1980.

He was a plain speaker with a gift for putting large ideas into simple words. He believed that communism was doomed by its own faults, and he was willing to say so openly. He also believed in talking with his enemies. He left office in 1989 and in 1994 announced that he had Alzheimer’s disease.

The Soviet Collapse

Detente, Afghanistan, Reagan, and Solidarity

Part 1

Detente and Afghanistan

Chapter 1Detente
Chapter 2Afghanistan
Chapter 1

Detente

By the late 1960s both sides were weary. The Vietnam War had drained America, and the Soviets, who had reached rough equality in nuclear weapons, were spending a huge part of their wealth on the arms race. President Nixon and his adviser Henry Kissinger sought a calmer relationship, which they called détente. In 1972 Nixon went to Beijing and met Mao, and the opening to China left Moscow uneasy. The same year, he and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the first arms-limitation treaty, SALT I, and a treaty that limited antimissile defenses. Trade grew, and astronauts of the two countries docked their spacecraft in orbit in 1975.

In 1975 thirty-five nations, including the United States, Canada, and every European state but Albania, signed the Helsinki Final Act. The Soviets wanted the agreement because it recognized the borders set after the war. The West wanted it because it also pledged respect for human rights and for the self-determination of peoples. The Soviets thought that they had won, but it gave courage to dissidents, who formed groups in Moscow, Prague, and Warsaw to watch whether their governments kept the promise. Detente did not stop either side from competing. The Soviets backed Communist forces in Angola, Ethiopia, and Yemen. Americans asked why the Soviet buildup went on, and the arms race had not slowed.

Chapter 2

Afghanistan

In 1978 Communist officers took power in Afghanistan, a poor and mountainous country on the Soviet border, and began to remake it by force. They closed mosques and jailed tribal leaders, and the country rose in revolt. In December 1979 Soviet troops entered Kabul, killed the Afghan leader, and installed another. Brezhnev and a few advisers had decided that they could not allow a Communist neighbor to fall. They thought the war would be short.

It was not. The Soviet army, built to fight a war on the plains of Europe, could hold the cities but not the mountains. The Afghan rebels, the mujahideen, fought as guerrillas. They received arms from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and the United States. Millions of Afghans fled their homes and became refugees, most of them in Pakistan and Iran. President Carter called the invasion the greatest danger to peace since the Second World War. He halted the sale of American grain to the Soviet Union, withdrew the SALT II treaty from the Senate, and led a boycott of the Moscow Olympic Games in 1980, which about sixty other nations joined. In the end, about fifteen thousand Soviet soldiers died, and perhaps a million Afghans. The war cost the Soviets a great deal and gained them nothing.

Part 2

Poland and Solidarity

Chapter 3The Pope and the Shipyard
Chapter 4Martial Law
Chapter 3

The Pope and the Shipyard

Poland was the most restless of the Soviet satellites. Its people were devout Catholics, and the government had never beaten the Church. In October 1978 the cardinal of Krakow, Karol Wojtyla, was elected pope as John Paul II, the first non-Italian pope in over four hundred years. When he visited Poland in June 1979, millions came out to see him. He told them, “Be not afraid.” Many Poles said afterward that for the first time they saw how many of them there were.

In August 1980 workers struck at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk after a crane operator, Anna Walentynowicz, was fired. They were led by an electrician named Lech Walesa. The strike spread, and the government gave way and signed the Gdansk Agreement, which recognized the right to form an independent trade union. It was called Solidarnosc, or Solidarity. Within a year about ten million Poles had joined it, nearly one in three workers. A free union in a Communist state was something new, and both sides knew it could not last unless one side changed.

Chapter 4

Martial Law

In December 1980 the Soviet leaders discussed an invasion and decided against it, as Afghanistan was already costing too much. On December 13, 1981, Poland’s own leader, General Wojciech Jaruzelski, declared martial law. Soldiers arrested thousands of Solidarity’s leaders, and the union was banned. Poland was kept quiet, but it was not conquered. The union’s members went underground, the Church sheltered them, and the Pope visited again in 1983. The government had learned that it could rule by force but not by consent. The tie between Polish nationalism and the Church was strong, and it was not broken.

Part 3

Reagan and the Pressures

Chapter 5Reagan and the New Cold War
Chapter 6What You Have Seen
Chapter 5

Reagan and the New Cold War

Ronald Reagan was elected in November 1980 on a promise to rebuild American strength. Reagan thought that detente had left the United States weaker, and he believed that the Soviet system was fragile. He increased defense spending sharply and ordered new missiles for Europe. In March 1983 he called the Soviet Union an evil empire. A few weeks later he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, a plan to build a defense against missiles. Critics called it Star Wars, and Soviet leaders feared that it might give America a way to strike first. In September 1983 a Soviet fighter shot down a Korean airliner that had strayed into Soviet air space, and 269 people died.

The tension was real. In November 1983 NATO held a war game that the Soviet leaders, who were old and suspicious, seem to have feared might be a cover for a real attack. Historians still argue about how close this brought the world to danger. Reagan also said that nuclear war could not be won and must never be fought, and that he would meet any Soviet leader who would talk seriously. He had also given aid to the mujahideen and, quietly, to Solidarity. He was helped by the fact that, in the Soviet Union, the leaders died one after another. Brezhnev died in 1982, and two aging successors died in quick turn. In March 1985 the Politburo chose a man of fifty-four.

Chapter 6

What You Have Seen

Look at the list you started. Some pressures came from outside, such as the American buildup and the cost of Afghanistan. Some came from within: a slow economy, an aging leadership, and peoples who did not wish to be ruled. In the next lesson you will meet the man who tried to answer these pressures, and you will see what happened to his answer.
